✨ The key to your baby’s sleep schedule? It’s all about knowing their cues! Understanding the difference between sleepy, tired, and overtired can make all the difference:

💤 Sleepy: Just the right time to settle down for a nap or bedtime. Look for subtle yawns, calm movements, or zoning out.

😴 Tired: They’re ready for sleep but may need some help winding down. You’ll see more rubbing of the eyes or fussiness.

😩 Overtired: They’ve passed their sweet spot. Cue meltdowns, difficulty falling asleep, and needing extra soothing.

Mastering these cues = smoother sleep transitions for both you and your baby! 🍼💤

Teaching kids about money doesn’t have to be complicated — or boring 💵

My aunt had the most amazing game she played with us and her kids growing up that turned grocery shopping from mundane to a competition. The end result? We learned the cost of every day goods and everyone’s mental math improved. 

Next time you’re in the grocery store, try this game 👇

Each child keeps a running total of your cart in their head. No phones. No calculators.

When you get to the checkout, whoever’s closest to the total picks the shared treat! 🍫

It’s a simple way to make money sense a part of everyday life, and sneak in a little mental math, too. 😉

If your kids are older, make it a little harder by adding the total needs to be after-tax!

This was my 8 year old daughter’s gymnastics summer camp morning routine. She had just learned how to pony tail her hair and how to hand wrap, but doing them both together on her own was new and took long. Setting out the items she needed in order made it so she was confident to try it by herself. 

Don’t be afraid to go back to basics- use visual tools to make multi-step tasks easier for your kids. Take baby steps to help them feel confident before expecting them to be independent. 

Some extra insights:
➡️ even if you think they “know” how to do a task, visual reminders can still go a long way in making the task more fluid
➡️ start small. You might try this for one part of your multi-step routine, eg in this example maybe just starting with the pony tail steps rather than merging 2 tasks together 
➡️ let them talk through their steps before they start the task- explaining their steps and thought process before can help boost their follow through

Parent Hack Thursday!
According to Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, children need to feel safe, calm, and connected before they can focus on academics. That’s where SEL and mindfulness come in.

Try reading an SEL story, such as Breathe Like a Bear, with your child. Afterward, guide them through a quick mindfulness practice, like taking three deep breaths together.

Why it works: Meeting social-emotional needs first strengthens a child’s sense of safety and belonging. In turn, this boosts focus, comprehension, and vocabulary growth when they read.

Meeting emotional needs first leads to stronger academic success.

There is so much hype around summer as we scroll social media (90’s summer anyone?!), and I won’t lie that I am excited for the summer pace, sunshine late into the evening, and running out the door in sandals!  However, the shifts in routines and exciting events can also tip the balance of our days, particularly for our children who have sensory sensitivities and/or deeply felt emotional responses. 

Though we all need a different balance of experiences to feel regulated, being aware of which areas may start to tip your child’s equilibrium can help you build in some buffers in other areas to help them (and in return yourself) stay a bit more balanced this summer! If social interactions can be draining for your child, consider prepping them with a plan and space to take a break, no matter what grandma thinks they should be doing next.  Throw in a chewy and noise cancelling headphones for your sensitive child on planes, sporting events, and fireworks. 

All of this is easier said than done and we are learning, often the hard way, the value of planning and pacing around our children’s particular needs for balance. Sometimes we get it right, a slow morning in a beach house with time for independent play before a long beach afternoon. Sometimes the extra ice cream stop was clearly one thing too many.

Parent hack for reducing waste from wet wipes and net reduction of plastic packaging. We can’t claim original credit for this great way of reducing plastics involved in baby wipes but it’s a great #parenthack . You’ll need a roll of paper towel (makes two batches), a plastic container big enough to fit 1/2 roll of paper towel, jab saw, olive oil, organic baby wash, tablespoon measure, kettle to boil water and measuring cup. We normally use #whogivesacrap paper towel but they won’t deliver to our new country house so we’ve been buying the largest number of paper towels in one package from supermarket until we find a workaround. 
1. Cut paper towel in half with jab saw on chopping board.

2. Boil water in kettle.

3. Add 1 tablespoon of olive oil and 1 tablespoon of organic baby wash to measuring jug.

4. Top up to 250ml with boiling water (1 cup for those of you in the United States) and pour over paper towel in your plastic container. Let soak through for 10 minutes and remove cardboard roll. Voila! Cheap eco (low plastic) baby wipes! 
Also better for your kids skin as you’re not using the alcohol in baby wipes on their skin. 
P.S. These baby wipes (just like store bought baby wipes) *can’t be flushed down the toilet* but because they are made completely from paper you could potentially compost them if you have a composting and worm farm setup, hence reducing landfill further.

PARENT HACK: Little kid in grown up situations...
Think religious holidays, weddings, dinner out at a fancy restaurant, a 95th birthday celebration. 
It seems like once our little ones surpass the age of 3 (when society says tantrums are no longer acceptable), they are ‘expected’ to be tiny little adults when out in public. And we as parents (me included) feel the pressure for our kids to perform! To say Hello politely, to smile, make conversation, sit nicely at the table, eat with their mouths closed, have calm bodies and keep their indoor voices on! 
Ack!!! It’s too much!

Today this little peanut was thrown into this exact position... and I was kind of nervous walking in, but she nailed it! Ok, ok she may have asked me over 22 times when the cake was coming out, and I may have wanted to pull my hair out because of it but overall, she played the role of ‘mini adult’ like a pro. *** ‘Played the role?’ Yep! Here’s how it worked: leading up to this event we role played what it would be like at an adult party, in a fun and engaging session of imaginary play. It was then that together we discussed appropriate vs. inappropriate behaviours when at a dinner. She LOVED this time with me. We set the table, got dressed up and had some yummy snacks, pretending to be adults! Then today, on our way to our adult party, we reminisced about our recent imaginary party and decided we would ‘do it, just like we did at home!’ Why am I telling you this? In hopes that it helps you!! When children understand what they are walking into and what is expected of them they have an easier time meeting our expectations. 
Tip: Make a secret signal together, a tap on the nose or a secret word like UNICORNS for your child to use when they feel like they just can’t sit still for one more minute. When they use the signal, excuse yourselves from the table and take a quick walk to the bathroom to have a moment of silly together before returning back. It’s ok to take breaks!

Parent Hack: Enjoy a candy-free Halloween! 🎃 🍂
Instead of overloading the little one with tons of candy, try these fun alternatives to keep the Halloween spirit alive without the sugar rush.

👻 Halloween-Themed Goodie Bags: Fill bags with non-candy treats like stickers, glow sticks, temporary tattoos, or fun pencils. Kids love collecting these goodies just as much as candy!

🎃 DIY Pumpkin Decorating Kits: Instead of sweets, give out small pumpkins with art supplies (markers, stickers, and paint) for kids to decorate at home. It’s a creative way to celebrate!

🎨 Fall Crafts and Activities: Hand out mini craft kits or activity sheets with Halloween-themed crafts. This keeps kids entertained and encourages creativity.

🍎 Healthy Treats: Consider giving out fun fruit snacks, popcorn balls, or homemade trail mix. You can even make it festive by using Halloween-themed packaging!

🔍 Spooky Scavenger Hunt: Organize a neighborhood scavenger hunt with Halloween-themed items to find instead of candy. Kids will have a blast hunting for treats!
By getting creative with your Halloween treats, you can make the holiday just as special without the candy overload! 🙌
